a: On the third day Esther dressed herself as queen.
t: Addition D: Esther before the king (1)
p: The Greek replaces 5:1–2 with a long, dramatic scene, Addition D. This entry and the one on 5:2 go together.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV and modern Protestant and Jewish versions
readings.orig: וַיְהִי בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי וַתִּלְבַּשׁ אֶסְתֵּר מַלְכוּת
readings.en: and it was on the third day, and Esther put on royalty
readings.plain: On the third day Esther dressed herself as queen.

readings.w: Septuagint, the main Greek text (the 'B-text'; Rahlfs; Göttingen edition, Hanhart), 5:1a–f (Addition D 1–6); the Greek Alpha Text has a similar scene
readings.orig: καὶ ἐγενήθη ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ τρίτῃ ... περιεβάλετο τὴν δόξαν αὐτῆς
readings.en: on the third day ... she clothed herself in her glory
readings.plain: On the third day Esther took off the clothes she had prayed in and dressed herself in her glory. [Greek Addition D (5:1a–f) adds: she takes two maids, one to hold up her train; she is radiant, but her heart is frozen with fear. She passes through every door and stands before the king, who sits on his throne in his robes, covered in gold and precious stones. He looks up, his face burning with glory, in fierce anger. The queen turns pale and faints on the maid who goes before her.]

why: The Additions are not part of the Hebrew Bible. Additions B and E were composed in Greek; A, C, D and F, including this one, probably go back to a Hebrew or Aramaic original (Moore; Martin). All six are part of Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians, whose older Bibles print it in chapter 15, following the Vulgate's order. The Plain follows the Hebrew; the Greek is summarized here.
b: Addition D is the emotional climax of the Greek book. Where the Hebrew gives two calm sentences, the Greek shows Esther's terror, the king's anger and, in the next verse, God turning the king's heart. It follows Addition C, the prayers of Mordecai and Esther, which come after 4:17. Rahlfs prints it as 5:1a–f and 5:2a–b. Jerome moved all the Additions to the end of his Latin Esther, which is why older Catholic Bibles print this passage in chapter 15.

a: she gained his favor
t: Addition D: Esther before the king (2)
p: In the Greek, God changes the king's spirit to gentleness, the king springs up and holds her, and she faints again. Goes with the entry on 5:1.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV and modern Protestant and Jewish versions
readings.en: she lifted up favor in his eyes
readings.plain: she gained his favor

readings.w: Septuagint, the main Greek text (the 'B-text'; Rahlfs; Göttingen edition, Hanhart), 5:1e–2b (Addition D 8–16)
readings.orig: καὶ μετέβαλεν ὁ θεὸς τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ βασιλέως εἰς πραΰτητα
readings.en: and God changed the spirit of the king to gentleness
readings.plain: God changed the king's spirit to gentleness. [Greek Addition D adds: the king leaps from his throne in alarm, takes her in his arms until she comes to, and comforts her: 'I am your brother. Take courage. You will not die, for our law is only for ordinary people.' He touches her neck with the gold scepter and kisses her. She tells him she saw him like an angel of God and her heart was shaken by his glory, and she faints again while all his servants try to comfort her.]

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. The Greek wording "God changed the spirit of the king" is the first place in the main story where the Greek names God's action at this moment; the Hebrew says only that Esther "gained his favor."
b: Here the two forms of the book differ most sharply in what they say about God. The Hebrew never names him; the Greek makes him the cause of the king's change of heart. Fox and others think the Greek translator added the Additions partly to make the religious meaning explicit.

t: "Because the living God is with him"
p: The Greek adds a reason to the advisers' warning: the living God is with Mordecai.

readings.plain: For the slanderer is not worthy of the king's court.

why: The Greek translator seems to have read tsar as "enemy" and rendered the clause freely; Haman is "the slanderer" (diabolos) again in 8:1. The Plain keeps the Hebrew and gives its readings in the note.

a: Harbona
p: The Hebrew names the eunuch Harbona, as in 1:10. The Septuagint names him Bougathan, the Alpha Text Agathas.

readings.plain: Agathas

why: Greek Esther often gives different forms of the Persian names. Bougathan may be a confusion with Bigthan of 2:21. The Plain follows the Hebrew, which ties this eunuch to the one sent for Vashti in 1:10. In the Greek the king's order is "let him be crucified" (staurōthētō), and then Haman "was hanged" (ekremasthē).

a: It was the twenty-third day of the third month, Sivan.
p: The Hebrew dates the letter to 23 Sivan, the third month. The Greek has 23 Nisan, the first month.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV and modern Protestant and Jewish versions
readings.orig: בַּחֹדֶשׁ הַשְּׁלִישִׁי הוּא־חֹדֶשׁ סִיוָן בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁה וְעֶשְׂרִים בּוֹ
readings.en: in the third month, that is the month of Sivan, on its twenty-third
readings.plain: It was the twenty-third day of the third month, Sivan.

readings.w: Septuagint, the main Greek text (the 'B-text'; Rahlfs; Göttingen edition, Hanhart)
readings.orig: ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ μηνί, ὅς ἐστιν Νισα, τρίτῃ καὶ εἰκάδι
readings.en: in the first month, which is Nisa, on the twenty-third
readings.plain: It was the twenty-third day of the first month, Nisan.

why: The Hebrew is the harder and more specific date, and leaves a gap of about seventy days after Haman's letter of 13 Nisan (3:12). The Greek date, ten days after Haman's letter, would put the whole of chapters 4–8 within ten days. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: little children and women, and their property could be taken as plunder
p: The Hebrew mirrors Haman's decree (3:13). The Greek lets the Jews keep their own laws and deal with their enemies as they wish, with no mention of women, children or plunder.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV and modern Protestant and Jewish versions
readings.en: little ones and women, and their spoil to plunder
readings.plain: little children and women, and their property could be taken as plunder

readings.w: Septuagint, the main Greek text (the 'B-text'; Rahlfs; Göttingen edition, Hanhart)
readings.orig: χρῆσθαι τοῖς νόμοις αὐτῶν ... χρήσασθαι τοῖς ἀντιδίκοις αὐτῶν ... ὡς βούλονται
readings.en: to use their own laws ... to deal with their opponents ... as they wish
readings.plain: and they could treat their opponents and enemies as they wished

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew, whose wording deliberately reverses 3:13. The Greek version is milder and stresses the Jews' right to live by their own laws, a concern of Greek-speaking Jews in Egypt.

a: the thirteenth of the twelfth month, Adar.
t: Addition E: the king's second letter
p: After 8:12 the Greek gives the full text of the king's new letter, Addition E. The Hebrew only reports it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV and modern Protestant and Jewish versions
readings.orig: בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁה עָשָׂר לְחֹדֶשׁ שְׁנֵים־עָשָׂר הוּא־חֹדֶשׁ אֲדָר
readings.en: on the thirteenth of the twelfth month, that is the month of Adar
readings.plain: the thirteenth of the twelfth month, Adar.

readings.w: Septuagint, the main Greek text (the 'B-text'; Rahlfs; Göttingen edition, Hanhart), 8:12a–x (Addition E 1–24); the Alpha Text has a form of it too
readings.en: The great King Artaxerxes ...
readings.plain: the thirteenth of the twelfth month, Adar. [Greek Addition E adds the letter itself: 'The great King Artaxerxes' writes to the governors of the 127 satrapies that some men abuse the kindness of kings. Haman son of Hammedatha, a Macedonian, a foreigner with no Persian blood, whom the king had honored as 'our father,' plotted to destroy Mordecai, the king's savior, and Esther, his blameless queen, and their whole nation, so as to hand the kingdom to the Macedonians. But the Jews are not evildoers; they live by most just laws and are children of the Most High, the most mighty living God. The officials are not to carry out Haman's letters. Haman has been crucified at the gates of Susa with his household, God having quickly paid him back. Copies are to be posted everywhere, the Jews may live by their own laws, and they are to be helped on the 13th of Adar. The day is to be kept as a feast, and any city that disobeys will be destroyed.]

why: Addition E, like Addition B (Haman's letter after 3:13), is written in polished Greek court style and was almost certainly composed in Greek. It is not part of the Hebrew Bible. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include it (Vulgate 16:1–24). The Plain follows the Hebrew and summarizes the addition here.
b: Two features stand out. Haman becomes a "Macedonian" (also in the Greek of 9:24), which turns him into a Greek plotting against Persia, a charge that would have meant something in Ptolemaic Egypt. And a pagan king confesses the God of the Jews as "the Most High, the most mighty living God," something the Hebrew king never does.

a: made themselves Jews
p: The Greek says many of the nations "were circumcised and lived as Jews."

readings.en: many of the Jews were circumcised
readings.plain: were circumcised (said of Jews, not of the peoples of the land)

why: The Greek takes the rare Hebrew verb as full conversion. Josephus also speaks of circumcision, but done "out of fear of the Jews" to make themselves safe (Antiquities 11.285). The Alpha Text speaks of Jews, not gentiles, being circumcised. The Hebrew word allows other readings (see the note). The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: So the Jews cut down all their enemies. It was a blow of the sword, of slaughter and destruction. They treated those who hated them however they wanted.
p: The Septuagint as printed by Rahlfs has nothing for 9:5.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV and modern Protestant and Jewish versions

readings.en: and the Jews struck all their enemies ... and did to those hating them as they wished
readings.plain: So the Jews cut down all their enemies. It was a blow of the sword, of slaughter and destruction. They treated those who hated them however they wanted.

readings.w: Septuagint, the main Greek text (the 'B-text'; Rahlfs; Göttingen edition, Hanhart) (no text for this verse)

why: The verse is in all Hebrew manuscripts. Its absence from the Greek is probably the translator's choice, one of several places where the Greek shortens the account of the fighting (compare 9:10 and 9:16). The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: But they kept their hands off the plunder.
p: The Hebrew says the Jews did not touch the plunder. The Greek of 9:10 says "and they plundered."

why: The Hebrew repeats the refusal three times (9:10, 15, 16), and the Greek itself has "they plundered nothing" in 9:15 and 9:16, so its reading here stands alone and may come from the decree's permission in 8:11. The Plain follows the Hebrew, which is consistent with its own pattern.

t: Pur or "a decree and a lot"?
p: The Hebrew explains the Persian-Babylonian word Pur. The Greek has "he made a decree and a lot," and calls Haman "the Macedonian."

why: The Greek drops the foreign word, as it calls the festival by another name in 9:26. The Plain follows the Hebrew, which keeps the word that explains the festival's name.

p: The Greek calls the festival Phrourai, "because of the lots, for in their language they are called Phrourai."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV and modern Protestant and Jewish versions
readings.en: Purim, on account of the name of the Pur
readings.plain: Purim, from the name Pur

readings.w: Septuagint, the main Greek text (the 'B-text'; Rahlfs; Göttingen edition, Hanhart)
readings.orig: Φρουραι διὰ τοὺς κλήρους ὅτι τῇ διαλέκτῳ αὐτῶν καλοῦνται Φρουραι
readings.en: Phrourai, because of the lots, for in their language they are called Phrourai

why: Phrourai is probably a Greek form of the Hebrew or Aramaic name, perhaps influenced by Greek phroura, "guard." The colophon after 10:3 speaks of the "letter of Phrourai" (see the variant on 10:3). The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: Abihail's daughter
p: The Greek names Esther's father Aminadab, as it does in 2:15.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV and modern Protestant and Jewish versions
readings.en: daughter of Abihail
readings.plain: Abihail's daughter

readings.w: Septuagint, the main Greek text (the 'B-text'; Rahlfs; Göttingen edition, Hanhart)
readings.en: daughter of Aminadab
readings.plain: Aminadab's daughter

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew, which uses the same name in 2:15. Aminadab is a familiar biblical name (Exodus 6:23; Ruth 4:19), and a Greek copyist or translator may have put it in place of the rarer Abihail.

a: spoke peace to all his offspring.
p: The Greek book ends with Addition F, in which Mordecai explains his dream, and a note about who brought the Greek translation to Egypt.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV and modern Protestant and Jewish versions
readings.en: and speaking peace to all his seed
readings.plain: spoke peace to all his offspring.

readings.w: Septuagint, the main Greek text (the 'B-text'; Rahlfs; Göttingen edition, Hanhart), 10:3a–k (Addition F) and the colophon (10:3l)
readings.en: These things have come from God ...
readings.plain: spoke peace to all his offspring. [Greek Addition F adds: Mordecai says, 'These things have come from God.' He recalls the dream of Addition A, before chapter 1: the little spring that became a river, with light and sun and much water, is Esther, whom the king married and made queen; the two dragons are Haman and himself; the nations gathered to destroy the name of the Jews; his nation is Israel, who cried out to God and were saved. God made two lots, one for the people of God and one for the nations, and the hour of decision came, and God remembered his people and vindicated his inheritance. These days, the 14th and 15th of Adar, are to be kept with joy before God forever. The colophon follows: 'In the fourth year of the reign of Ptolemy and Cleopatra,' Dositheus, who said he was a priest and a Levite, and his son Ptolemy brought (to Egypt) this letter about Phrourai, which they said was genuine and had been translated by Lysimachus son of Ptolemy, one of the people in Jerusalem.]

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew, which ends with Mordecai's greatness. Addition F and the colophon are not in any Hebrew manuscript. Addition F gives the whole Greek book a frame (with Addition A) and states its theology: the lots were God's.
b: The colophon is one of the few dated notes in the Greek Bible. Which Ptolemy and Cleopatra are meant is debated: Elias Bickerman argued for Ptolemy XII and Cleopatra V, which gives 78/77 BC; others prefer Ptolemy IX with Cleopatra III (114/113 BC) or Ptolemy XIII with Cleopatra VII (49/48 BC). On any of these dates, the note claims that the Greek Esther was made in Jerusalem and brought to Egypt to promote Purim among Greek-speaking Jews.

a: The enemies of the Jews had hoped that on this day they would rule over them. But it was turned upside down. The Jews themselves ruled over those who hated them.
p: The Septuagint has no "turned upside down". Its 9:1 says only that the king's letters arrived; 9:2 adds that the Jews' opponents perished.

readings.plain: The letters written by the king arrived.

why: The Hebrew's two words venahafokh hu, "it was turned upside down," state the book's theme; the Greek translator, who often shortens the fighting, leaves them out. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

p: In the Septuagint the second day is "so as to hang" Haman's sons. In the Alpha Text Esther asks that the Jews may destroy and plunder whom they wish.

readings.orig: δοθήτω τοῖς Ιουδαίοις χρῆσθαι ὡσαύτως τὴν αὔριον ὥστε τοὺς δέκα υἱοὺς κρεμάσαι Αμαν

why: The Hebrew gives two requests and no motive. The Septuagint ties the extra day to the display of the bodies. The Alpha Text, which also gives larger numbers (700 in Susa, 70,100 in the kingdom), has a harsher request that allows plunder, the opposite of the Hebrew's threefold refusal (9:10, 15, 16). a: But when the matter came before the king, he gave orders in writing: the evil plot Haman had plotted against the Jews must come back on his own head, and he and his sons must be hung on the pole.
p: The Septuagint makes Haman the one who went in to the king, to ask for Mordecai's hanging.

readings.orig: וּבְבֹאָהּ לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ אָמַר עִם־הַסֵּפֶר יָשׁוּב מַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ הָרָעָה
readings.en: and when she/it came before the king, he said with the letter: let his evil plot return
readings.plain: But when the matter came before the king, he gave orders in writing: the evil plot Haman had plotted against the Jews must come back on his own head, and he and his sons must be hung on the pole.

readings.w: Septuagint, the main Greek text (the 'B-text'; Rahlfs; Göttingen edition, Hanhart)
readings.orig: καὶ ὡς εἰσῆλθεν πρὸς τὸν βασιλέα ... ἐκρεμάσθη αὐτὸς καὶ τὰ τέκνα αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and how he went in to the king, saying to hang Mordecai ... he was hanged, he and his children
readings.plain: And Haman went in to the king, asking that Mordecai be hanged. But the evils he tried to bring on the Jews came on him, and he was hanged, he and his children.

why: The Hebrew's feminine "when she/it came" is ambiguous (see the note); the Greek resolves it by making Haman the subject, which fits 6:4. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

why: The Greek is obscure here and may reflect a different or damaged text. The Hebrew is in all Hebrew manuscripts, and the Plain follows it. The difference matters because the Fast of Esther rests on the Hebrew wording.
